=================== index.adoc
     1	:stylus: https://docs.arbitrum.io/stylus/gentle-introduction[Stylus]
     2	
     3	= OpenZeppelin Contracts for Stylus
     4	
     5	*A secure, modular smart contract library for {stylus}, written in Rust.*
     6	
     7	OpenZeppelin Contracts for Stylus brings time-tested smart contract patterns to Arbitrum’s WASM-based execution environment. This library provides `no_std`-compatible modules for building secure, reusable contracts in {stylus}.
     8	
     9	== Features
    10	
    11	- ✨ Security-first contracts ported from https://github.com/OpenZeppelin/openzeppelin-contracts[`openzeppelin-contracts`].
    12	- 📦 Written in Rust with full `no_std` support.
    13	- 🧪 Tested with both unit and integration tests.
    14	- 🚧 Actively developed.
    15	
    16	== Quick Start
    17	
    18	Add the dependency to your `Cargo.toml`:
    19	
    20	[source,toml]
    21	----
    22	[dependencies]
    23	openzeppelin-stylus = "=0.3.0"
    24	----
    25	
    26	Enable the ABI export feature:
    27	
    28	[source,toml]
    29	----
    30	[features]
    31	export-abi = ["openzeppelin-stylus/export-abi"]
    32	----
    33	
    34	== Usage Example
    35	
    36	A minimal ERC-20 implementation using the library:
    37	
    38	[source,rust]
    39	----
    40	use openzeppelin_stylus::token::erc20::{self, Erc20, IErc20};
    41	use stylus_sdk::{
    42	    alloy_primitives::{Address, U256},
    43	    prelude::*,
    44	};
    45	
    46	#[entrypoint]
    47	#[storage]
    48	struct Erc20Example {
    49	    erc20: Erc20,
    50	}
    51	
    52	#[public]
    53	#[implements(IErc20<Error = erc20::Error>)]
    54	impl Erc20Example {}
    55	
    56	#[public]
    57	impl IErc20 for Erc20Example {
    58	    // ERC-20 logic implementation...
    59	}
    60	----
    61	
    62	Explore more examples in the https://github.com/OpenZeppelin/rust-contracts-stylus/tree/main/examples[`examples` directory].
    63	
    64	== Compatibility
    65	
    66	This library is designed to work with `no_std`. To keep your contracts compatible, disable default features for any dependencies that pull in the standard library:
    67	
    68	[source,toml]
    69	----
    70	[dependencies]
    71	alloy-primitives = { version = "=0.8.20", default-features = false }
    72	stylus-sdk = "=0.9.0"
    73	----
    74	
    75	== Roadmap & Contributing
    76	
    77	See what’s planned or in development in our https://github.com/orgs/OpenZeppelin/projects/35[roadmap].
    78	
    79	Interested in contributing? Read the https://github.com/OpenZeppelin/rust-contracts-stylus/blob/main/CONTRIBUTING.md[contribution guide].
    80	
    81	== Security
    82	
    83	While this library is under active development, security remains a top priority. For past audits and security reports, see the https://github.com/OpenZeppelin/rust-contracts-stylus/tree/main/audits[`audits` directory].
    84	
    85	== License
    86	
    87	Released under the https://github.com/OpenZeppelin/rust-contracts-stylus/blob/main/LICENSE[MIT License].
=================== tokens.adoc
     1	= Tokens
     2	
     3	Ah, the "token": blockchain's most powerful and most misunderstood tool.
     4	
     5	A token is a _representation of something in the blockchain_. This something can be money, time, services, shares in a company, a virtual pet, anything. By representing things as tokens, we can allow smart contracts to interact with them, exchange them, create or destroy them.
     6	
     7	[[but_first_coffee_a_primer_on_token_contracts]]
     8	== But First, [strikethrough]#Coffee# a Primer on Token Contracts
     9	
    10	Much of the confusion surrounding tokens comes from two concepts getting mixed up: _token contracts_ and the actual _tokens_.
    11	
    12	A _token contract_ is simply an Ethereum smart contract. "Sending tokens" actually means "calling a method on a smart contract that someone wrote and deployed". At the end of the day, a token contract is not much more than a mapping of addresses to balances, plus some methods to add and subtract from those balances.
    13	
    14	It is these balances that represent the _tokens_ themselves. Someone "has tokens" when their balance in the token contract is non-zero. That's it! These balances could be considered money, experience points in a game, deeds of ownership, or voting rights, and each of these tokens would be stored in different token contracts.
    15	
    16	[[different-kinds-of-tokens]]
    17	== Different Kinds of Tokens
    18	
    19	Note that there's a big difference between having two voting rights and two deeds of ownership: each vote is equal to all others, but houses usually are not! This is called https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fungibility[fungibility]. _Fungible goods_ are equivalent and interchangeable, like Ether, fiat currencies, and voting rights. _Non-fungible_ goods are unique and distinct, like deeds of ownership, or collectibles.
    20	
    21	In a nutshell, when dealing with non-fungibles (like your house) you care about _which ones_ you have, while in fungible assets (like your bank account statement) what matters is _how much_ you have.
    22	
    23	== Standards
    24	
    25	Even though the concept of a token is simple, they have a variety of complexities in the implementation. Because everything in Ethereum is just a smart contract, and there are no rules about what smart contracts have to do, the community has developed a variety of *standards* (called EIPs or ERCs) for documenting how a contract can interoperate with other contracts.
    26	
    27	You've probably heard of the ERC-20, ERC-721 or ERC-1155 token standards, and that's why you're here. Head to our specialized guides to learn more about these:
    28	
    29	 * xref:erc20.adoc[ERC-20]: the most widespread token standard for fungible assets, albeit somewhat limited by its simplicity.
    30	 * xref:erc721.adoc[ERC-721]: the de-facto solution for non-fungible tokens, often used for collectibles and games.
    31	 * xref:erc1155.adoc[ERC-1155]: a novel standard for multi-tokens, allowing for a single contract to represent multiple fungible and non-fungible tokens, along with batched operations for increased gas efficiency.
=================== utilities.adoc
     1	= Utilities
     2	
     3	The OpenZeppelin Stylus Contracts provides a ton of useful utilities that you can use in your project.
     4	For a complete list, check out the https://docs.rs/openzeppelin-stylus/0.3.0/openzeppelin_stylus/utils/index.html[API Reference].
     5	Here are some of the more popular ones.
     6	
     7	[[introspection]]
     8	== Introspection
     9	
    10	It's frequently helpful to know whether a contract supports an interface you'd like to use.
    11	https://eips.ethereum.org/EIPS/eip-165[`ERC-165`] is a standard that helps do runtime interface detection.
    12	Contracts for Stylus provides helpers for implementing ERC-165 in your contracts:
    13	
    14	* https://docs.rs/openzeppelin-stylus/0.3.0/openzeppelin_stylus/utils/introspection/erc165/trait.IErc165.html[`IERC165`] — this is the ERC-165 trait that defines https://docs.rs/openzeppelin-stylus/0.3.0/openzeppelin_stylus/utils/introspection/erc165/trait.IErc165.html#tymethod.supports_interface[`supportsInterface`]. In order to implement ERC-165 interface detection, you should manually expose https://docs.rs/openzeppelin-stylus/0.3.0/openzeppelin_stylus/utils/introspection/erc165/trait.IErc165.html#tymethod.supports_interface[`supportsInterface`] function in your contract.
    15	
    16	[source,rust]
    17	----
    18	#[entrypoint]
    19	#[storage]
    20	struct Erc721Example {
    21	    erc721: Erc721,
    22	}
    23	
    24	#[public]
    25	#[implements(IErc721<Error = Error>, IErc165)]
    26	impl Erc721Example {
    27	    // ...
    28	}
    29	
    30	#[public]
    31	impl IErc165 for Erc721Example {
    32	    fn supports_interface(&self, interface_id: B32) -> bool {
    33	        self.erc721.supports_interface(interface_id)
    34	    }
    35	}
    36	
    37	#[public]
    38	impl IErc721 for Erc721Example {
    39	    // ...
    40	}
    41	----
    42	
    43	[[structures]]
    44	== Structures
    45	
    46	Some use cases require more powerful data structures than arrays and mappings offered natively in `alloy` and the Stylus SDK.
    47	Contracts for Stylus provides these libraries for enhanced data structure management:
    48	
    49	- https://docs.rs/openzeppelin-stylus/0.3.0/openzeppelin_stylus/utils/structs/bitmap/index.html[`BitMaps`]: Store packed booleans in storage.
    50	- https://docs.rs/openzeppelin-stylus/0.3.0/openzeppelin_stylus/utils/structs/checkpoints/index.html[`Checkpoints`]: Checkpoint values with built-in lookups.
    51	- https://docs.rs/openzeppelin-stylus/0.3.0/openzeppelin_stylus/utils/structs/enumerable_set/index.html[`EnumerableSets`]: Contract for managing sets of many primitive types.
=================== crypto.adoc
     1	= Crypto
     2	
     3	The OpenZeppelin Rust Contracts provide a crate for common cryptographic procedures in a blockchain environment. The following documents the available functionality.
     4	
     5	== Verifying Merkle Proofs
     6	
     7	Developers can build a Merkle Tree off-chain, which allows for verifying that an element (leaf) is part of a set by using a Merkle Proof. This technique is widely used for creating whitelists (e.g. for airdrops) and other advanced use cases.
     8	
     9	TIP: OpenZeppelin Contracts provides a https://github.com/OpenZeppelin/merkle-tree[JavaScript library] for building trees off-chain and generating proofs.
    10	
    11	https://docs.rs/openzeppelin-crypto/0.3.0/openzeppelin_crypto/merkle/struct.Verifier.html[`MerkleProof`] provides:
    12	
    13	* https://docs.rs/openzeppelin-crypto/0.3.0/openzeppelin_crypto/merkle/struct.Verifier.html#method.verify[`verify`] - can prove that some value is part of a https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Merkle_tree[Merkle tree].
    14	
    15	* https://docs.rs/openzeppelin-crypto/0.3.0/openzeppelin_crypto/merkle/struct.Verifier.html#method.verify_multi_proof[`verify_multi_proof`] - can prove multiple values are part of a Merkle tree.
    16	
    17	[source,rust]
    18	----
    19	fn verify(&self, proof: Vec<B256>, root: B256, leaf: B256) -> bool {
    20	    let proof: Vec<[u8; 32]> = proof.into_iter().map(|m| *m).collect();
    21	    Verifier::<KeccakBuilder>::verify(&proof, *root, *leaf)
    22	}
    23	----
    24	
    25	Note that these functions use `keccak256` as the hashing algorithm, but our library also provides generic counterparts: https://docs.rs/openzeppelin-crypto/0.3.0/openzeppelin_crypto/merkle/struct.Verifier.html#method.verify_with_builder[`verify_with_builder`] and https://docs.rs/openzeppelin-crypto/0.3.0/openzeppelin_crypto/merkle/struct.Verifier.html#method.verify_multi_proof_with_builder[`verify_multi_proof_with_builder`].
    26	
    27	We also provide an adapter https://docs.rs/openzeppelin-crypto/0.3.0/openzeppelin_crypto/hash/index.html[`hash`] module to use your own hashers in conjunction with them that resembles Rust's standard library's API.
=================== finance.adoc
     1	= Finance
     2	
     3	Contracts that include primitives for financial systems.
     4	
     5	== VestingWallet
     6	* xref:vesting-wallet.adoc[VestingWallet] handles the vesting of Ether and ERC-20
     7	  tokens for a given beneficiary. Custody of multiple tokens can be given to this
     8	  contract, which will release the token to the beneficiary following a given,
     9	  customizable, vesting schedule.
=================== common.adoc
     1	= Common (Tokens)
     2	
     3	Contracts that are common to multiple token standards.
     4	
     5	== ERC-2981
     6	* *https://eips.ethereum.org/EIPS/eip-2981[ERC-2981]*: standardized way to retrieve royalty payment information for non-fungible tokens (NFTs) to enable universal support for royalty payments across all NFT marketplaces and ecosystem participants.
=================== erc1155.adoc
     1	= ERC-1155
     2	
     3	ERC1155 is a novel token standard that aims to take the best from previous standards to create a xref:tokens.adoc#different-kinds-of-tokens[*fungibility-agnostic*] and *gas-efficient* xref:tokens.adoc#but_first_coffee_a_primer_on_token_contracts[token contract].
     4	
     5	[[erc1155-token-extensions]]
     6	== Extensions
     7	
     8	Additionally, there are multiple custom extensions, including:
     9	
    10	* xref:erc1155-burnable.adoc[ERC-1155 Burnable]: Optional Burnable extension of the ERC-1155 standard.
    11	
    12	* xref:erc1155-metadata-uri.adoc[ERC-1155 Metadata URI]: Optional extension that adds a token metadata URI.
    13	
    14	* xref:erc1155-pausable.adoc[ERC-1155 Pausable]: A primitive to pause contract operation like token transfers, minting and burning.
    15	
    16	* xref:erc1155-uri-storage.adoc[ERC-1155 URI Storage]: A more flexible but more expensive way of storing URI metadata.
    17	
    18	* xref:erc1155-supply.adoc[ERC-1155 Supply]: Extension of the ERC-1155 standard that adds tracking of total supply per token id.
=================== erc2981.adoc
     1	= ERC-2981
     2	
     3	ERC-2981 offers a way to keep track of NFT royalties across different platforms.
     4	
     5	Royalty is the amount of money given to the owner of a particular asset (NFT in this case). Full definition: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Royalty_payment [royalty].
     6	
     7	This makes ERC-2981 useful for keeping track of royalty information across different platforms. It ensures that users don't have to specify this information on every platform, and the information remains transparent on the blockchain.
     8	
     9	== Limitations and Considerations
    10	
    11	- **Marketplace Enforcement**: Some NFT marketplaces may not enforce royalties.
    12	- **Manual Distribution**: On-chain royalty tracking does not mean automatic payouts.
    13	- **Gas Costs**: Extra storage and computations can slightly increase gas fees.
    14	
    15	== Additional Resources
    16	
    17	- ERC-2981 EIP: https://eips.ethereum.org/EIPS/eip-2981[EIP-2981 Specification]

content.content:
=================== erc20.adoc
     1	= ERC-20
     2	
     3	An ERC-20 token contract keeps track of xref:tokens.adoc#different-kinds-of-tokens[_fungible_ tokens]: any token is exactly equal to any other token; no token has a special right or behavior associated with them.
     4	This makes ERC-20 tokens useful for things like a *medium of exchange currency*, *voting rights*, *staking*, and more.
     5	
     6	OpenZeppelin Contracts provide many ERC20-related contracts for Arbitrum Stylus.
     7	On the https://docs.rs/openzeppelin-stylus/0.3.0/openzeppelin_stylus/token/erc20/struct.Erc20.html[`API reference`] you'll find detailed information on their properties and usage.
     8	
     9	[[constructing-an-erc20-token-contract]]
    10	== Constructing an ERC-20 Token Contract
    11	
    12	Using Contracts, we can easily create our own ERC-20 token contract, which will be used to track _Gold_ (GLD), an internal currency in a hypothetical game.
    13	
    14	Here's what our GLD token might look like.
    15	
    16	[source,rust]
    17	----
    18	use openzeppelin_stylus::{
    19	    token::erc20::{
    20	        self,
    21	        extensions::{Erc20Metadata, IErc20Metadata},
    22	        Erc20, IErc20,
    23	    },
    24	};
    25	
    26	#[entrypoint]
    27	#[storage]
    28	struct GLDToken {
    29	    erc20: Erc20,
    30	    metadata: Erc20Metadata,
    31	}
    32	
    33	#[public]
    34	#[implements(IErc20<Error = erc20::Error>, IErc20Metadata, IErc165)]
    35	impl GLDToken {
    36	    #[constructor]
    37	    fn constructor(&mut self, name: String, symbol: String) {
    38	        self.metadata.constructor(name, symbol);
    39	    }
    40	
    41	    // ...
    42	}
    43	
    44	#[public]
    45	impl IErc20 for GLDToken {
    46	    type Error = erc20::Error;
    47	
    48	    fn total_supply(&self) -> U256 {
    49	        self.erc20.total_supply()
    50	    }
    51	
    52	    fn balance_of(&self, account: Address) -> U256 {
    53	        self.erc20.balance_of(account)
    54	    }
    55	
    56	    fn transfer(
    57	        &mut self,
    58	        to: Address,
    59	        value: U256,
    60	    ) -> Result<bool, Self::Error> {
    61	        self.erc20.transfer(to, value)
    62	    }
    63	
    64	    fn allowance(&self, owner: Address, spender: Address) -> U256 {
    65	        self.erc20.allowance(owner, spender)
    66	    }
    67	
    68	    fn approve(
    69	        &mut self,
    70	        spender: Address,
    71	        value: U256,
    72	    ) -> Result<bool, Self::Error> {
    73	        self.erc20.approve(spender, value)
    74	    }
    75	
    76	    fn transfer_from(
    77	        &mut self,
    78	        from: Address,
    79	        to: Address,
    80	        value: U256,
    81	    ) -> Result<bool, Self::Error> {
    82	        self.erc20.transfer_from(from, to, value)
    83	    }
    84	}
    85	
    86	#[public]
    87	impl IErc20Metadata for GLDToken {
    88	    fn name(&self) -> String {
    89	        self.metadata.name()
    90	    }
    91	
    92	    fn symbol(&self) -> String {
    93	        self.metadata.symbol()
    94	    }
    95	
    96	    fn decimals(&self) -> U8 {
    97	        self.metadata.decimals()
    98	    }
    99	}
   100	
   101	#[public]
   102	impl IErc165 for GLDToken {
   103	    fn supports_interface(&self, interface_id: B32) -> bool {
   104	        self.erc20.supports_interface(interface_id)
   105	            || self.metadata.supports_interface(interface_id)
   106	    }
   107	}
   108	----
   109	
   110	Our contracts are often used via stylus-sdk https://docs.arbitrum.io/stylus/reference/rust-sdk-guide#inheritance-inherit-and-borrow[inheritance], and here we're reusing https://docs.rs/openzeppelin-stylus/0.3.0/openzeppelin_stylus/token/erc20/struct.Erc20.html[`ERC20`] for both the basic standard implementation and with optional extensions.
   111	
   112	[[a-note-on-decimals]]
   113	== A Note on `decimals`
   114	
   115	Often, you'll want to be able to divide your tokens into arbitrary amounts: say, if you own `5 GLD`, you may want to send `1.5 GLD` to a friend, and keep `3.5 GLD` to yourself.
   116	Unfortunately, Solidity and the EVM do not support this behavior: only integer (whole) numbers can be used, which poses an issue.
   117	You may send `1` or `2` tokens, but not `1.5`.
   118	
   119	To work around this, ERC20 provides a https://docs.rs/openzeppelin-stylus/0.3.0/openzeppelin_stylus/token/erc20/extensions/metadata/trait.IErc20Metadata.html#tymethod.decimals[`decimals`] field, which is used to specify how many decimal places a token has.
   120	To be able to transfer `1.5 GLD`, `decimals` must be at least `1`, since that number has a single decimal place.
   121	
   122	How can this be achieved?
   123	It's actually very simple: a token contract can use larger integer values, so that a balance of `50` will represent `5 GLD`, a transfer of `15` will correspond to `1.5 GLD` being sent, and so on.
   124	
   125	It is important to understand that `decimals` is _only used for display purposes_.
   126	All arithmetic inside the contract is still performed on integers, and it is the different user interfaces (wallets, exchanges, etc.) that must adjust the displayed values according to `decimals`.
   127	The total token supply and balance of each account are not specified in `GLD`: you need to divide by `10 ** decimals` to get the actual `GLD` amount.
   128	
   129	You'll probably want to use a `decimals` value of `18`, just like Ether and most ERC-20 token contracts in use, unless you have an exceptional reason not to.
   130	When minting tokens or transferring them around, you will be actually sending the number `GLD * (10 ** decimals)`.
   131	
   132	NOTE: By default, `ERC20` uses a value of `18` for `decimals`.
   133	
   134	To use a different value, you will need to override the `decimals()` function in your contract. For example, to use `16` decimals, you would do:
   135	
   136	[source,rust]
   137	----
   138	fn decimals(&self) -> U8 {
   139	    U8::from(16)
   140	}
   141	----
   142	
   143	So if you want to send `5` tokens using a token contract with `18` decimals, the method to call will actually be:
   144	
   145	[source,rust]
   146	----
   147	token.transfer(recipient, 5 * uint!(10_U256).pow(uint!(18_U256)));
   148	----
   149	
   150	[[erc20-token-extensions]]
   151	== Extensions
   152	Additionally, there are multiple custom extensions, including:
   153	
   154	 * xref:erc20-burnable.adoc[ERC-20 Burnable]: destruction of own tokens.
   155	
   156	 * xref:erc20-capped.adoc[ERC-20 Capped]: enforcement of a cap to the total supply when minting tokens.
   157	
   158	 * xref:erc20-metadata.adoc[ERC-20 Metadata]: the extended ERC20 interface including the name, symbol, and decimals functions.
   159	
   160	 * xref:erc20-pausable.adoc[ERC-20 Pausable]: ability to pause token transfers.
   161	
   162	 * xref:erc20-permit.adoc[ERC-20 Permit]: gasless approval of tokens (standardized as https://eips.ethereum.org/EIPS/eip-2612[`EIP-2612`]).
   163	
   164	 * xref:erc4626.adoc[ERC-4626]: tokenized vault that manages shares (represented as ERC-20) that are backed by assets (another ERC-20).
   165	
   166	 * xref:erc20-flash-mint.adoc[ERC-20 Flash-Mint]: token level support for flash loans through the minting and burning of ephemeral tokens (standardized as https://eips.ethereum.org/EIPS/eip-3156[`EIP-3156`]).
   167	
   168	 * xref:erc20-wrapper.adoc[ERC-20 Wrapper]: wrapper to create an ERC-20 backed by another ERC-20, with deposit and withdraw methods.
=================== erc20-burnable.adoc
     1	= ERC-20 Burnable
     2	
     3	Extension of xref:erc20.adoc[ERC-20] that allows token holders to destroy both their own tokens and those that they have an allowance for, in a way that can be recognized off-chain (via event analysis).
     4	
     5	[[usage]]
     6	== Usage
     7	
     8	In order to make https://docs.rs/openzeppelin-stylus/0.3.0/openzeppelin_stylus/token/erc20/extensions/burnable/index.html[`ERC-20 Burnable`] methods “external” so that other contracts can call them, you need to implement them by yourself for your final contract as follows:
     9	
    10	[source,rust]
    11	----
    12	use openzeppelin_stylus::token::erc20::{
    13	    self, extensions::IErc20Burnable, Erc20, IErc20,
    14	};
    15	
    16	#[entrypoint]
    17	#[storage]
    18	struct Erc20Example {
    19	    erc20: Erc20,
    20	}
    21	
    22	#[public]
    23	#[implements(IErc20<Error = erc20::Error>, IErc20Burnable<Error = erc20::Error>)]
    24	impl Erc20Example {}
    25	
    26	
    27	#[public]
    28	impl IErc20 for Erc20Example {
    29	    type Error = erc20::Error;
    30	
    31	    fn total_supply(&self) -> U256 {
    32	        self.erc20.total_supply()
    33	    }
    34	
    35	    fn balance_of(&self, account: Address) -> U256 {
    36	        self.erc20.balance_of(account)
    37	    }
    38	
    39	    fn transfer(
    40	        &mut self,
    41	        to: Address,
    42	        value: U256,
    43	    ) -> Result<bool, Self::Error> {
    44	        self.erc20.transfer(to, value)
    45	    }
    46	
    47	    fn allowance(&self, owner: Address, spender: Address) -> U256 {
    48	        self.erc20.allowance(owner, spender)
    49	    }
    50	
    51	    fn approve(
    52	        &mut self,
    53	        spender: Address,
    54	        value: U256,
    55	    ) -> Result<bool, Self::Error> {
    56	        self.erc20.approve(spender, value)
    57	    }
    58	
    59	    fn transfer_from(
    60	        &mut self,
    61	        from: Address,
    62	        to: Address,
    63	        value: U256,
    64	    ) -> Result<bool, Self::Error> {
    65	        self.erc20.transfer_from(from, to, value)
    66	    }
    67	}
    68	
    69	
    70	#[public]
    71	impl IErc20Burnable for Erc20Example {
    72	    type Error = erc20::Error;
    73	
    74	    fn burn(&mut self, value: U256) -> Result<(), erc20::Error> {
    75	        // ...
    76	        self.erc20.burn(value)
    77	    }
    78	
    79	    fn burn_from(
    80	        &mut self,
    81	        account: Address,
    82	        value: U256,
    83	    ) -> Result<(), erc20::Error> {
    84	        // ...
    85	        self.erc20.burn_from(account, value)
    86	    }
    87	}
    88	----
=================== erc20-capped.adoc
     1	= ERC-20 Capped
     2	
     3	Extension of xref:erc20.adoc[ERC-20] that adds a cap to the supply of tokens.
     4	
     5	[[usage]]
     6	== Usage
     7	
     8	In order to make https://docs.rs/openzeppelin-stylus/0.3.0/openzeppelin_stylus/token/erc20/extensions/capped/index.html[`ERC-20 Capped`] methods supervising the supply of tokens, you need to add them by yourself for your final contract as follows:
     9	
    10	[source,rust]
    11	----
    12	use openzeppelin_stylus::token::erc20::{
    13	    self,
    14	    extensions::{capped, Capped, ICapped},
    15	    Erc20, IErc20,
    16	};
    17	
    18	#[derive(SolidityError, Debug)]
    19	enum Error {
    20	    ExceededCap(capped::ERC20ExceededCap),
    21	    InvalidCap(capped::ERC20InvalidCap),
    22	    InsufficientBalance(erc20::ERC20InsufficientBalance),
    23	    InvalidSender(erc20::ERC20InvalidSender),
    24	    InvalidReceiver(erc20::ERC20InvalidReceiver),
    25	    InsufficientAllowance(erc20::ERC20InsufficientAllowance),
    26	    InvalidSpender(erc20::ERC20InvalidSpender),
    27	    InvalidApprover(erc20::ERC20InvalidApprover),
    28	}
    29	
    30	impl From<capped::Error> for Error {
    31	    fn from(value: capped::Error) -> Self {
    32	        match value {
    33	            capped::Error::ExceededCap(e) => Error::ExceededCap(e),
    34	            capped::Error::InvalidCap(e) => Error::InvalidCap(e),
    35	        }
    36	    }
    37	}
    38	
    39	impl From<erc20::Error> for Error {
    40	    fn from(value: erc20::Error) -> Self {
    41	        match value {
    42	            erc20::Error::InsufficientBalance(e) => {
    43	                Error::InsufficientBalance(e)
    44	            }
    45	            erc20::Error::InvalidSender(e) => Error::InvalidSender(e),
    46	            erc20::Error::InvalidReceiver(e) => Error::InvalidReceiver(e),
    47	            erc20::Error::InsufficientAllowance(e) => {
    48	                Error::InsufficientAllowance(e)
    49	            }
    50	            erc20::Error::InvalidSpender(e) => Error::InvalidSpender(e),
    51	            erc20::Error::InvalidApprover(e) => Error::InvalidApprover(e),
    52	        }
    53	    }
    54	}
    55	
    56	#[entrypoint]
    57	#[storage]
    58	struct Erc20Example {
    59	    erc20: Erc20,
    60	    capped: Capped,
    61	}
    62	
    63	#[public]
    64	#[implements(IErc20<Error = Error>, ICapped)]
    65	impl Erc20Example {
    66	    #[constructor]
    67	    fn constructor(&mut self, cap: U256) -> Result<(), Error> {
    68	        Ok(self.capped.constructor(cap)?)
    69	    }
    70	
    71	    // Add token minting feature.
    72	    //
    73	    // Make sure to handle `Capped` properly. You should not call
    74	    // [`Erc20::_update`] to mint tokens -- it will break the `Capped`
    75	    // mechanism.
    76	    fn mint(
    77	        &mut self,
    78	        account: Address,
    79	        value: U256,
    80	    ) -> Result<(), Error> {
    81	        let max_supply = self.capped.cap();
    82	
    83	        // Overflow check required.
    84	        let supply = self
    85	            .erc20
    86	            .total_supply()
    87	            .checked_add(value)
    88	            .expect("new supply should not exceed `U256::MAX`");
    89	
    90	        if supply > max_supply {
    91	            return Err(capped::Error::ExceededCap(
    92	                capped::ERC20ExceededCap {
    93	                    increased_supply: supply,
    94	                    cap: max_supply,
    95	                },
    96	            ))?;
    97	        }
    98	
    99	        self.erc20._mint(account, value)?;
   100	        Ok(())
   101	    }
   102	}
   103	
   104	#[public]
   105	impl ICapped for Erc20Example {
   106	    fn cap(&self) -> U256 {
   107	        self.capped.cap()
   108	    }
   109	}
   110	
   111	#[public]
   112	impl IErc20 for Erc20Example {
   113	    type Error = Error;
   114	
   115	    fn total_supply(&self) -> U256 {
   116	        self.erc20.total_supply()
   117	    }
   118	
   119	    fn balance_of(&self, account: Address) -> U256 {
   120	        self.erc20.balance_of(account)
   121	    }
   122	
   123	    fn transfer(
   124	        &mut self,
   125	        to: Address,
   126	        value: U256,
   127	    ) -> Result<bool, Self::Error> {
   128	        Ok(self.erc20.transfer(to, value)?)
   129	    }
   130	
   131	    fn allowance(&self, owner: Address, spender: Address) -> U256 {
   132	        self.erc20.allowance(owner, spender)
   133	    }
   134	
   135	    fn approve(
   136	        &mut self,
   137	        spender: Address,
   138	        value: U256,
   139	    ) -> Result<bool, Self::Error> {
   140	        Ok(self.erc20.approve(spender, value)?)
   141	    }
   142	
   143	    fn transfer_from(
   144	        &mut self,
   145	        from: Address,
   146	        to: Address,
   147	        value: U256,
   148	    ) -> Result<bool, Self::Error> {
   149	        Ok(self.erc20.transfer_from(from, to, value)?)
   150	    }
   151	}

1	//! Permit Contract.
2	//!
3	//! Extension of the ERC-20 standard allowing approvals to be made
4	//! via signatures, as defined in the [ERC].
5	//!
6	//! Adds the `permit` method, which can be used to change an account’s
7	//! ERC20 allowance (see [`crate::token::erc20::IErc20::allowance`])
8	//! by presenting a message signed by the account.
9	//! By not relying on [`erc20::IErc20::approve`],
10	//! the token holder account doesn’t need to send a transaction,
11	//! and thus is not required to hold Ether at all.
12	//!
13	//! [ERC]: https://eips.ethereum.org/EIPS/eip-2612
14	
15	use alloc::{vec, vec::Vec};
16	
17	use alloy_primitives::{aliases::B32, keccak256, Address, B256, U256, U8};
18	use alloy_sol_types::SolType;
19	use stylus_sdk::{
20	    function_selector, prelude::*, stylus_core::calls::errors::MethodError,
21	};
22	
23	use crate::{
24	    token::erc20::{self, Erc20},
25	    utils::{
26	        cryptography::eip712::IEip712,
27	        nonces::{INonces, Nonces},
28	        precompiles::{
29	            primitives::ecrecover::{
30	                self, ECDSAInvalidSignature, ECDSAInvalidSignatureS,
31	            },
32	            Precompiles,
33	        },
34	    },
35	};
36	
37	const PERMIT_TYPEHASH: [u8; 32] =
38	    keccak_const::Keccak256::new()
39	        .update(b"Permit(address owner,address spender,uint256 value,uint256 nonce,uint256 deadline)")
40	        .finalize();
41	
42	pub use sol::*;
43	#[cfg_attr(coverage_nightly, coverage(off))]
44	mod sol {
45	    use alloy_sol_macro::sol;
46	
47	    pub(crate) type StructHashTuple = sol! {
48	        tuple(bytes32, address, address, uint256, uint256, uint256)
49	    };
50	
51	    sol! {
52	        /// Indicates an error related to the fact that
53	        /// permit deadline has expired.
54	        #[derive(Debug)]
55	        #[allow(missing_docs)]
56	        error ERC2612ExpiredSignature(uint256 deadline);
57	
58	        /// Indicates an error related to the issue about mismatched signature.
59	        #[derive(Debug)]
60	        #[allow(missing_docs)]
61	        error ERC2612InvalidSigner(address signer, address owner);
62	    }
63	}
64	
65	/// A Permit error.
66	#[derive(SolidityError, Debug)]
67	pub enum Error {
68	    /// Indicates an error related to the fact that
69	    /// permit deadline has expired.
70	    ExpiredSignature(ERC2612ExpiredSignature),
71	    /// Indicates an error related to the issue about mismatched signature.
72	    InvalidSigner(ERC2612InvalidSigner),
73	    /// Indicates an error related to the current balance of `sender`. Used in
74	    /// transfers.
75	    InsufficientBalance(erc20::ERC20InsufficientBalance),
76	    /// Indicates a failure with the token `sender`. Used in transfers.
77	    InvalidSender(erc20::ERC20InvalidSender),
78	    /// Indicates a failure with the token `receiver`. Used in transfers.
79	    InvalidReceiver(erc20::ERC20InvalidReceiver),
80	    /// Indicates a failure with the `spender`’s `allowance`. Used in
81	    /// transfers.
82	    InsufficientAllowance(erc20::ERC20InsufficientAllowance),
83	    /// Indicates a failure with the `spender` to be approved. Used in
84	    /// approvals.
85	    InvalidSpender(erc20::ERC20InvalidSpender),
86	    /// Indicates a failure with the `approver` of a token to be approved. Used
87	    /// in approvals. approver Address initiating an approval operation.
88	    InvalidApprover(erc20::ERC20InvalidApprover),
89	    /// The signature derives the [`Address::ZERO`].
90	    InvalidSignature(ECDSAInvalidSignature),
91	    /// The signature has an `S` value that is in the upper half order.
92	    InvalidSignatureS(ECDSAInvalidSignatureS),
93	}
94	
95	impl From<erc20::Error> for Error {
96	    fn from(value: erc20::Error) -> Self {
97	        match value {
98	            erc20::Error::InsufficientBalance(e) => {
99	                Error::InsufficientBalance(e)
100	            }
101	            erc20::Error::InvalidSender(e) => Error::InvalidSender(e),
102	            erc20::Error::InvalidReceiver(e) => Error::InvalidReceiver(e),
103	            erc20::Error::InsufficientAllowance(e) => {
104	                Error::InsufficientAllowance(e)
105	            }
106	            erc20::Error::InvalidSpender(e) => Error::InvalidSpender(e),
107	            erc20::Error::InvalidApprover(e) => Error::InvalidApprover(e),
108	        }
109	    }
110	}
111	
112	impl From<ecrecover::Error> for Error {
113	    fn from(value: ecrecover::Error) -> Self {
114	        match value {
115	            ecrecover::Error::InvalidSignature(e) => Error::InvalidSignature(e),
116	            ecrecover::Error::InvalidSignatureS(e) => {
117	                Error::InvalidSignatureS(e)
118	            }
119	        }
120	    }
121	}
122	
123	impl MethodError for Error {
124	    fn encode(self) -> alloc::vec::Vec<u8> {
125	        self.into()
126	    }
127	}
128	
129	/// State of an [`Erc20Permit`] Contract.
130	#[storage]
131	pub struct Erc20Permit<T: IEip712 + StorageType> {
132	    /// Contract implementing [`IEip712`] trait.
133	    pub(crate) eip712: T,
134	}
135	
136	/// NOTE: Implementation of [`TopLevelStorage`] to be able use `&mut self` when
137	/// calling other contracts and not `&mut (impl TopLevelStorage +
138	/// BorrowMut<Self>)`. Should be fixed in the future by the Stylus team.
139	unsafe impl<T: IEip712 + StorageType> TopLevelStorage for Erc20Permit<T> {}
140	
141	/// Interface for [`Erc20Permit`]
142	#[public]
143	// The `#[public]` macro adds an undocumented helper method to the trait.
144	#[allow(missing_docs)]
145	pub trait IErc20Permit: INonces {
146	    /// The error type associated to this interface.
147	    type Error: Into<alloc::vec::Vec<u8>>;
148	
149	    // Calculated manually to include [`INonces::nonces`].
150	    /// Solidity interface id associated with [`IErc20Permit`] trait.
151	    /// Computed as a XOR of selectors for each function in the trait.
152	    #[must_use]
153	    fn interface_id() -> B32
154	    where
155	        Self: Sized,
156	    {
157	        B32::new(function_selector!("DOMAIN_SEPARATOR",))
158	            ^ B32::new(function_selector!("nonces", Address,))
159	            ^ B32::new(function_selector!(
160	                "permit", Address, Address, U256, U256, U8, B256, B256
161	            ))
162	    }
163	
164	    /// Returns the domain separator used in the encoding of the signature for
165	    /// [`Self::permit`], as defined by EIP712.
166	    ///
167	    /// NOTE: The implementation should use `#[selector(name =
168	    /// "DOMAIN_SEPARATOR")]` to match Solidity's camelCase naming
169	    /// convention.
170	    ///
171	    /// # Arguments
172	    ///
173	    /// * `&self` - Read access to the contract's state.
174	    #[must_use]
175	    fn domain_separator(&self) -> B256;
176	
177	    /// Sets `value` as the allowance of `spender` over `owner`'s tokens,
178	    /// given `owner`'s signed approval.
179	    ///
180	    /// # Arguments
181	    ///
182	    /// * `&mut self` - Write access to the contract's state. given address.
183	    /// * `owner` - Account that owns the tokens.
184	    /// * `spender` - Account that will spend the tokens.
185	    /// * `value` - The number of tokens being permitted to transfer by
186	    ///   `spender`.
187	    /// * `deadline` - Deadline for the permit action.
188	    /// * `v` - v value from the `owner`'s signature.
189	    /// * `r` - r value from the `owner`'s signature.
190	    /// * `s` - s value from the `owner`'s signature.
191	    ///
192	    /// # Errors
193	    ///
194	    /// * [`ERC2612ExpiredSignature`] - If the `deadline` param is from the
195	    ///   past.
196	    /// * [`ERC2612InvalidSigner`] - If signer is not an `owner`.
197	    /// * [`ecrecover::Error::InvalidSignatureS`] - If the `s` value is grater
198	    ///   than [`ecrecover::SIGNATURE_S_UPPER_BOUND`].
199	    /// * [`ecrecover::Error::InvalidSignature`] - If the recovered address is
200	    ///   [`Address::ZERO`].
201	    /// * [`erc20::Error::InvalidSpender`] - If the `spender` address is
202	    ///   [`Address::ZERO`].
203	    ///
204	    /// # Events
205	    ///
206	    /// * [`erc20::Approval`]
207	    #[allow(clippy::too_many_arguments)]
208	    fn permit(
209	        &mut self,
210	        owner: Address,
211	        spender: Address,
212	        value: U256,
213	        deadline: U256,
214	        v: u8,
215	        r: B256,
216	        s: B256,
217	    ) -> Result<(), Self::Error>;
218	}
219	
220	impl<T: IEip712 + StorageType> Erc20Permit<T> {
221	    /// See [`IErc20Permit::domain_separator`].
222	    #[must_use]
223	    pub fn domain_separator(&self) -> B256 {
224	        self.eip712.domain_separator_v4()
225	    }
226	
227	    /// See [`IErc20Permit::permit`].
228	    #[allow(clippy::too_many_arguments, clippy::missing_errors_doc)]
229	    pub fn permit(
230	        &mut self,
231	        owner: Address,
232	        spender: Address,
233	        value: U256,
234	        deadline: U256,
235	        v: u8,
236	        r: B256,
237	        s: B256,
238	        erc20: &mut Erc20,
239	        nonces: &mut Nonces,
240	    ) -> Result<(), Error> {
241	        if U256::from(self.vm().block_timestamp()) > deadline {
242	            return Err(ERC2612ExpiredSignature { deadline }.into());
243	        }
244	
245	        let struct_hash = keccak256(StructHashTuple::abi_encode(&(
246	            PERMIT_TYPEHASH,
247	            owner,
248	            spender,
249	            value,
250	            nonces.use_nonce(owner),
251	            deadline,
252	        )));
253	
254	        let hash: B256 = self.eip712.hash_typed_data_v4(struct_hash);
255	
256	        let signer: Address = self.ec_recover(hash, v, r, s)?;
257	
258	        if signer != owner {
259	            return Err(ERC2612InvalidSigner { signer, owner }.into());
260	        }
261	
262	        erc20._approve(owner, spender, value, true)?;
263	
264	        Ok(())
265	    }
266	}

1	//! `ArbOS` precompiles wrapper enabling easier invocation.
2	
3	use alloy_primitives::{Address, B256};
4	use primitives::ecrecover::Error;
5	use stylus_sdk::{host::VM, prelude::*};
6	
7	use crate::utils::cryptography::ecdsa::recover;
8	
9	mod p256_verify;
10	
11	use p256_verify::p256_verify;
12	pub use p256_verify::P256_VERIFY_ADDRESS;
13	
14	/// Precompile primitives.
15	pub mod primitives {
16	    /// The `ecRecover` precompile primitives.
17	    ///
18	    /// This module provides the cryptographic primitives needed for the
19	    /// `ecRecover` precompile, which recovers the signer address from an
20	    /// ECDSA signature and message hash.
21	    ///
22	    /// Re-exports selected ECDSA types and constants specifically relevant
23	    /// to the ecrecover operation.
24	    pub mod ecrecover {
25	        pub use crate::utils::cryptography::ecdsa::{
26	            ECDSAInvalidSignature, ECDSAInvalidSignatureS, EcRecoverData,
27	            Error, ECRECOVER_ADDR, SIGNATURE_S_UPPER_BOUND,
28	        };
29	    }
30	}
31	
32	/// Trait providing access to Arbitrum precompiles for Stylus contracts.
33	///
34	/// This trait wraps complex precompile invocations to provide a clean,
35	/// ergonomic interface for calling Arbitrum's built-in cryptographic functions
36	/// and utilities from within Stylus smart contracts.
37	///
38	/// Precompiles are pre-deployed contracts at fixed addresses that implement
39	/// commonly used cryptographic operations and other utilities. They execute
40	/// natively in the Arbitrum runtime for better performance compared to
41	/// implementing these operations in contract code.
42	///
43	/// See: <https://docs.arbitrum.io/build-decentralized-apps/precompiles/overview>
44	///
45	/// # Usage
46	///
47	/// Implement this trait for your contract storage type to gain access to
48	/// precompile functionality:
49	///
50	/// ```rust,ignore
51	/// use openzeppelin_stylus::utils::precompiles::Precompiles;
52	///
53	/// #[storage]
54	/// #[entrypoint]
55	/// struct MyContract {
56	///     // your fields...
57	/// }
58	///
59	/// // The `Precompiles` trait is automatically implemented for all
60	/// // contracts annotated with `#[entrypoint]` or that implement
61	/// // `stylus_sdk::prelude::TopLevelStorage`, as long as they give access to
62	/// // the host through `stylus_sdk::prelude::HostAccess` (which `#[storage]`
63	/// // already provides).
64	///
65	/// #[public]
66	/// impl MyContract {
67	///     fn verify_signature(&mut self, msg_hash: B256, sig: (u8, B256, B256)) -> Result<Address, Error> {
68	///         let (v, r, s) = sig;
69	///         self.ec_recover(msg_hash, v, r, s)
70	///     }
71	/// }
72	/// ```
73	///
74	/// # Error Handling
75	///
76	/// Precompile methods return `Result` types to handle both invalid inputs and
77	/// precompile execution failures. Always handle these errors appropriately
78	/// in your contract logic.
79	pub trait Precompiles: TopLevelStorage + HostAccess<Host = VM> {
80	    /// Recovers the address that signed a hashed message (`hash`) using an
81	    /// ECDSA signature (v, r, s).
82	    ///
83	    /// Wrapper around the `ecRecover` precompile.
84	    ///
85	    /// # Arguments
86	    ///
87	    /// * `&self` - Read access to the contract's state.
88	    /// * `hash` - Hash of the message.
89	    /// * `v` - `v` value from the signature.
90	    /// * `r` - `r` value from the signature.
91	    /// * `s` - `s` value from the signature.
92	    ///
93	    /// # Errors
94	    ///
95	    /// * [`Error::InvalidSignatureS`] - If the `s` value is grater than
96	    ///   [`primitives::ecrecover::SIGNATURE_S_UPPER_BOUND`].
97	    /// * [`Error::InvalidSignature`] - If the recovered address is
98	    ///   [`Address::ZERO`].
99	    ///
100	    /// # Panics
101	    ///
102	    /// * If the `ecRecover` precompile fails to execute.
103	    fn ec_recover(
104	        &self,
105	        hash: B256,
106	        v: u8,
107	        r: B256,
108	        s: B256,
109	    ) -> Result<Address, Error>;
110	
111	    /// Performs signature verifications in the `secp256r1` elliptic curve.
112	    ///
113	    /// Wrapper around the `P256VERIFY` precompile introduced in [RIP-7212].
114	    ///
115	    /// [RIP-7212]: https://github.com/ethereum/RIPs/blob/723155c3d86427412b5bc0f98ad1e4791ea7347f/RIPS/rip-7212.md
116	    ///
117	    /// # Arguments
118	    ///
119	    /// * `&self` - Read access to the contract's state.
120	    /// * `hash` - Signed data hash.
121	    /// * `r` - `r` component of the signature.
122	    /// * `s` - `s` component of the signature.
123	    /// * `x` - `x` coordinate of the public key.
124	    /// * `y` - `y` coordinate of the public key.
125	    fn p256_verify(
126	        &self,
127	        hash: B256,
128	        r: B256,
129	        s: B256,
130	        x: B256,
131	        y: B256,
132	    ) -> bool;
133	}
134	
135	impl<T: TopLevelStorage + HostAccess<Host = VM>> Precompiles for T {
136	    fn ec_recover(
137	        &self,
138	        hash: B256,
139	        v: u8,
140	        r: B256,
141	        s: B256,
142	    ) -> Result<Address, Error> {
143	        recover(self, hash, v, r, s)
144	    }
145	
146	    fn p256_verify(
147	        &self,
148	        hash: B256,
149	        r: B256,
150	        s: B256,
151	        x: B256,
152	        y: B256,
153	    ) -> bool {
154	        p256_verify(self, hash, r, s, x, y)
155	    }
156	}

content.content:
=================== erc1155-burnable.adoc
     1	= ERC-1155 Burnable
     2	
     3	Extension of xref:erc1155.adoc[ERC-1155] that allows token holders to destroy both their
     4	own tokens and those that they have been approved to use.
     5	
     6	[[usage]]
     7	== Usage
     8	
     9	In order to make https://docs.rs/openzeppelin-stylus/0.3.0/openzeppelin_stylus/token/erc1155/extensions/burnable/index.html[`ERC-1155 Burnable`] methods “external” so that other contracts can call them, you need to implement them by yourself for your final contract as follows:
    10	
    11	[source,rust]
    12	----
    13	use openzeppelin_stylus::{
    14	    token::erc1155::{self, extensions::IErc1155Burnable, Erc1155, IErc1155},
    15	    utils::introspection::erc165::IErc165,
    16	};
    17	
    18	#[entrypoint]
    19	#[storage]
    20	struct Erc1155Example {
    21	    erc1155: Erc1155,
    22	}
    23	
    24	#[public]
    25	#[implements(IErc1155<Error = erc1155::Error>, IErc1155Burnable<Error = erc1155::Error>, IErc165)]
    26	impl Erc1155Example {
    27	    fn mint(
    28	        &mut self,
    29	        to: Address,
    30	        token_id: U256,
    31	        amount: U256,
    32	        data: Bytes,
    33	    ) -> Result<(), erc1155::Error> {
    34	        self.erc1155._mint(to, token_id, amount, &data)
    35	    }
    36	
    37	    fn mint_batch(
    38	        &mut self,
    39	        to: Address,
    40	        token_ids: Vec<U256>,
    41	        amounts: Vec<U256>,
    42	        data: Bytes,
    43	    ) -> Result<(), erc1155::Error> {
    44	        self.erc1155._mint_batch(to, token_ids, amounts, &data)
    45	    }
    46	}
    47	
    48	#[public]
    49	impl IErc1155Burnable for Erc1155Example {
    50	    type Error = erc1155::Error;
    51	
    52	    fn burn(
    53	        &mut self,
    54	        account: Address,
    55	        token_id: U256,
    56	        value: U256,
    57	    ) -> Result<(), erc1155::Error> {
    58	        // ...
    59	        self.erc1155.burn(account, token_id, value)?;
    60	        // ...
    61	        Ok(())
    62	    }
    63	
    64	    fn burn_batch(
    65	        &mut self,
    66	        account: Address,
    67	        token_ids: Vec<U256>,
    68	        values: Vec<U256>,
    69	    ) -> Result<(), erc1155::Error> {
    70	        // ...
    71	        self.erc1155.burn_batch(account, token_ids, values)?;
    72	        // ...
    73	        Ok(())
    74	    }
    75	}
    76	
    77	#[public]
    78	impl IErc1155 for Erc1155Example {
    79	    type Error = erc1155::Error;
    80	
    81	    fn balance_of(&self, account: Address, id: U256) -> U256 {
    82	        self.erc1155.balance_of(account, id)
    83	    }
    84	
    85	    fn balance_of_batch(
    86	        &self,
    87	        accounts: Vec<Address>,
    88	        ids: Vec<U256>,
    89	    ) -> Result<Vec<U256>, Self::Error> {
    90	        self.erc1155.balance_of_batch(accounts, ids)
    91	    }
    92	
    93	    fn set_approval_for_all(
    94	        &mut self,
    95	        operator: Address,
    96	        approved: bool,
    97	    ) -> Result<(), Self::Error> {
    98	        self.erc1155.set_approval_for_all(operator, approved)
    99	    }
   100	
   101	    fn is_approved_for_all(&self, account: Address, operator: Address) -> bool {
   102	        self.erc1155.is_approved_for_all(account, operator)
   103	    }
   104	
   105	    fn safe_transfer_from(
   106	        &mut self,
   107	        from: Address,
   108	        to: Address,
   109	        id: U256,
   110	        value: U256,
   111	        data: Bytes,
   112	    ) -> Result<(), Self::Error> {
   113	        self.erc1155.safe_transfer_from(from, to, id, value, data)
   114	    }
   115	
   116	    fn safe_batch_transfer_from(
   117	        &mut self,
   118	        from: Address,
   119	        to: Address,
   120	        ids: Vec<U256>,
   121	        values: Vec<U256>,
   122	        data: Bytes,
   123	    ) -> Result<(), Self::Error> {
   124	        self.erc1155.safe_batch_transfer_from(from, to, ids, values, data)
   125	    }
   126	}
   127	
   128	#[public]
   129	impl IErc165 for Erc1155Example {
   130	    fn supports_interface(&self, interface_id: B32) -> bool {
   131	        self.erc1155.supports_interface(interface_id)
   132	    }
   133	}
   134	----
=================== erc1155-metadata-uri.adoc
     1	= ERC-1155 Metadata URI
     2	
     3	The OpenZeppelin xref:erc1155.adoc[ERC-1155] Metadata URI extension is needed to manage and store URIs for individual tokens. This extension allows each token to have its own unique URI,
     4	which points to a JSON file that conforms to the https://eips.ethereum.org/EIPS/eip-1155#erc-1155-metadata-uri-json-schema[ERC-1155 Metadata URI JSON Schema].
     5	This is particularly useful for non-fungible tokens (NFTs) where each token is unique and may have different metadata.
     6	
     7	[[usage]]
     8	== Usage
     9	
    10	In order to make an xref:erc1155.adoc[ERC-1155] token with https://docs.rs/openzeppelin-stylus/0.3.0/openzeppelin_stylus/token/erc1155/extensions/metadata_uri/index.html[Metadata URI] flavour,
    11	you need to add the following code to your contract:
    12	
    13	[source,rust]
    14	----
    15	use openzeppelin_stylus::{
    16	    token::{
    17	        erc1155,
    18	        erc1155::{
    19	            extensions::{Erc1155MetadataUri, IErc1155MetadataUri},
    20	            Erc1155, IErc1155,
    21	        },
    22	    },
    23	    utils::introspection::erc165::IErc165,
    24	};
    25	
    26	#[entrypoint]
    27	#[storage]
    28	struct Erc1155MetadataUriExample {
    29	    erc1155: Erc1155,
    30	    metadata_uri: Erc1155MetadataUri,
    31	}
    32	
    33	#[public]
    34	#[implements(IErc1155<Error = erc1155::Error>, IErc1155MetadataUri, IErc165)]
    35	impl Erc1155MetadataUriExample {
    36	    #[constructor]
    37	    fn constructor(&mut self, uri: String) {
    38	        self.metadata_uri.constructor(uri);
    39	    }
    40	}
    41	
    42	#[public]
    43	impl IErc1155 for Erc1155MetadataUriExample {
    44	    type Error = erc1155::Error;
    45	
    46	    fn balance_of(&self, account: Address, id: U256) -> U256 {
    47	        self.erc1155.balance_of(account, id)
    48	    }
    49	
    50	    fn balance_of_batch(
    51	        &self,
    52	        accounts: Vec<Address>,
    53	        ids: Vec<U256>,

=================== access-control.adoc
     1	= Access Control
     2	
     3	Access control—that is, "who is allowed to do this thing"—is incredibly important in the world of smart contracts. The access control of your contract may govern who can mint tokens, vote on proposals, freeze transfers, and many other things. It is therefore *critical* to understand how you implement it, lest someone else https://blog.openzeppelin.com/on-the-parity-wallet-multisig-hack-405a8c12e8f7[steals your whole system].
     4	
     5	[[ownership-and-ownable]]
     6	== Ownership and `Ownable`
     7	
     8	The most common and basic form of access control is the concept of _ownership_: there's an account that is the `owner` of a contract and can do administrative tasks on it. This approach is perfectly reasonable for contracts that have a single administrative user.
     9	
    10	OpenZeppelin Contracts for Stylus provides https://docs.rs/openzeppelin-stylus/0.3.0/openzeppelin_stylus/access/ownable/struct.Ownable.html[`Ownable`] for implementing ownership in your contracts.
    11	
    12	[source,rust]
    13	----
    14	use openzeppelin_stylus::access::ownable::{self, Ownable};
    15	
    16	#[derive(SolidityError, Debug)]
    17	enum Error {
    18	    UnauthorizedAccount(ownable::OwnableUnauthorizedAccount),
    19	    InvalidOwner(ownable::OwnableInvalidOwner),
    20	    // other custom errors...
    21	}
    22	
    23	impl From<ownable::Error> for Error {
    24	    fn from(value: ownable::Error) -> Self {
    25	        match value {
    26	            ownable::Error::UnauthorizedAccount(e) => {
    27	                Error::UnauthorizedAccount(e)
    28	            }
    29	            ownable::Error::InvalidOwner(e) => Error::InvalidOwner(e),
    30	        }
    31	    }
    32	}
    33	
    34	#[entrypoint]
    35	#[storage]
    36	struct OwnableExample {
    37	    ownable: Ownable,
    38	}
    39	
    40	#[public]
    41	#[implements(IOwnable<Error = Error>)]
    42	impl MyContract {
    43	    fn normal_thing(&self) {
    44	        // anyone can call this normal_thing()
    45	    }
    46	
    47	    fn special_thing(&mut self) -> Result<(), Error> {
    48	        self.ownable.only_owner()?;
    49	
    50	        // only the owner can call special_thing()!
    51	
    52	        Ok(())
    53	    }
    54	}
    55	
    56	#[public]
    57	impl IOwnable for MyContract {
    58	    type Error = Error;
    59	
    60	    fn owner(&self) -> Address {
    61	        self.ownable.owner()
    62	    }
    63	
    64	    fn transfer_ownership(
    65	        &mut self,
    66	        new_owner: Address,
    67	    ) -> Result<(), Self::Error> {
    68	        Ok(self.ownable.transfer_ownership(new_owner)?)
    69	    }
    70	
    71	    fn renounce_ownership(&mut self) -> Result<(), Self::Error> {
    72	        Ok(self.ownable.renounce_ownership()?)
    73	    }
    74	}
    75	----
    76	
    77	At deployment, the https://docs.rs/openzeppelin-stylus/0.3.0/openzeppelin_stylus/access/ownable/struct.Ownable.html#method.owner[`owner`] of an `Ownable` contract is set to the provided `initial_owner` parameter.
    78	
    79	Ownable also lets you:
    80	
    81	* https://docs.rs/openzeppelin-stylus/0.3.0/openzeppelin_stylus/access/ownable/struct.Ownable.html#method.transfer_ownership[`transfer_ownership`] from the owner account to a new one, and
    82	* https://docs.rs/openzeppelin-stylus/0.3.0/openzeppelin_stylus/access/ownable/struct.Ownable.html#method.renounce_ownership[`renounce_ownership`] for the owner to relinquish this administrative privilege, a common pattern after an initial stage with centralized administration is over.
    83	
    84	WARNING: Removing the owner altogether will mean that administrative tasks that are protected by `only_owner` will no longer be callable!
    85	
    86	Note that *a contract can also be the owner of another one*! This opens the door to using, for example, a https://gnosis-safe.io[Gnosis Safe], an https://aragon.org[Aragon DAO], or a totally custom contract that _you_ create.
    87	
    88	In this way, you can use _composability_ to add additional layers of access control complexity to your contracts. Instead of having a single regular Ethereum account (Externally Owned Account, or EOA) as the owner, you could use a 2-of-3 multisig run by your project leads, for example. Prominent projects in the space, such as https://makerdao.com[MakerDAO], use systems similar to this one.
    89	
    90	
    91	[[role-based-access-control]]
    92	== Role-Based Access Control
    93	
    94	While the simplicity of _ownership_ can be useful for simple systems or quick prototyping, different levels of authorization are often needed. You may want for an account to have permission to ban users from a system, but not create new tokens. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Role-based_access_control[_Role-Based Access Control (RBAC)_] offers flexibility in this regard.
    95	
    96	In essence, we will be defining multiple _roles_, each allowed to perform different sets of actions. An account may have, for example, 'moderator', 'minter' or 'admin' roles, which you will then check for instead of simply using `only_owner`. This check can be enforced through the `only_role` modifier. Separately, you will be able to define rules for how accounts can be granted a role, have it revoked, and more.
    97	
    98	Most software uses access control systems that are role-based: some users are regular users, some may be supervisors or managers, and a few will often have administrative privileges.
    99	
   100	[[using-access-control]]
   101	=== Using `AccessControl`
   102	
   103	OpenZeppelin Contracts provides https://docs.rs/openzeppelin-stylus/0.3.0/openzeppelin_stylus/access/control/struct.AccessControl.html[`AccessControl`] for implementing role-based access control. Its usage is straightforward: for each role that you want to define,
   104	you will create a new _role identifier_ that is used to grant, revoke, and check if an account has that role.
   105	
   106	Here's a simple example of using `AccessControl` in an xref:erc20.adoc[ERC-20 token] to define a 'minter' role, which allows accounts that have it create new tokens. Note that the example is unassuming of the way you construct your contract.
   107	
   108	[source,rust]
   109	----
   110	use openzeppelin_stylus::{
   111	    access::control::{self, AccessControl, IAccessControl},
   112	    token::erc20::{self, Erc20, IErc20},
   113	};
   114	
   115	#[derive(SolidityError, Debug)]
   116	enum Error {
   117	    UnauthorizedAccount(control::AccessControlUnauthorizedAccount),
   118	    BadConfirmation(control::AccessControlBadConfirmation),
   119	    InsufficientBalance(erc20::ERC20InsufficientBalance),
   120	    InvalidSender(erc20::ERC20InvalidSender),
   121	    InvalidReceiver(erc20::ERC20InvalidReceiver),
   122	    InsufficientAllowance(erc20::ERC20InsufficientAllowance),
   123	    InvalidSpender(erc20::ERC20InvalidSpender),
   124	    InvalidApprover(erc20::ERC20InvalidApprover),
   125	}
   126	
   127	impl From<control::Error> for Error {
   128	    fn from(value: control::Error) -> Self {
   129	        match value {
   130	            control::Error::UnauthorizedAccount(e) => {
   131	                Error::UnauthorizedAccount(e)
   132	            }
   133	            control::Error::BadConfirmation(e) => Error::BadConfirmation(e),
   134	        }
   135	    }
   136	}
   137	
   138	impl From<erc20::Error> for Error {
   139	    fn from(value: erc20::Error) -> Self {
   140	        match value {
   141	            erc20::Error::InsufficientBalance(e) => {
   142	                Error::InsufficientBalance(e)
   143	            }
   144	            erc20::Error::InvalidSender(e) => Error::InvalidSender(e),
   145	            erc20::Error::InvalidReceiver(e) => Error::InvalidReceiver(e),
   146	            erc20::Error::InsufficientAllowance(e) => {
   147	                Error::InsufficientAllowance(e)
   148	            }
   149	            erc20::Error::InvalidSpender(e) => Error::InvalidSpender(e),
   150	            erc20::Error::InvalidApprover(e) => Error::InvalidApprover(e),
   151	        }
   152	    }
   153	}
   154	
   155	#[entrypoint]
   156	#[storage]
   157	struct Example {
   158	    erc20: Erc20,
   159	    access: AccessControl,
   160	}
   161	
   162	const MINTER_ROLE: [u8; 32] =
   163	    keccak_const::Keccak256::new().update(b"MINTER_ROLE").finalize();
   164	
   165	#[public]
   166	#[implements(IErc20<Error = Error>, IAccessControl<Error = Error>)]
   167	impl Example {
   168	    fn mint(&mut self, to: Address, amount: U256) -> Result<(), Error> {
   169	        self.access.only_role(MINTER_ROLE.into())?;
   170	        self.erc20._mint(to, amount)?;
   171	        Ok(())
   172	    }
   173	}
   174	
   175	#[public]
   176	impl IErc20 for Example {
   177	    type Error = Error;
   178	
   179	    fn total_supply(&self) -> U256 {
   180	        self.erc20.total_supply()
   181	    }
   182	
   183	    fn balance_of(&self, account: Address) -> U256 {
   184	        self.erc20.balance_of(account)
   185	    }
   186	
   187	    fn transfer(
   188	        &mut self,
   189	        to: Address,
   190	        value: U256,
   191	    ) -> Result<bool, Self::Error> {
   192	        Ok(self.erc20.transfer(to, value)?)
   193	    }
   194	
   195	    fn allowance(&self, owner: Address, spender: Address) -> U256 {
   196	        self.erc20.allowance(owner, spender)
   197	    }
   198	
   199	    fn approve(
   200	        &mut self,
   201	        spender: Address,
   202	        value: U256,
   203	    ) -> Result<bool, Self::Error> {
   204	        Ok(self.erc20.approve(spender, value)?)
   205	    }
   206	
   207	    fn transfer_from(
   208	        &mut self,
   209	        from: Address,
   210	        to: Address,
   211	        value: U256,
   212	    ) -> Result<bool, Self::Error> {
   213	        Ok(self.erc20.transfer_from(from, to, value)?)
   214	    }
   215	}
   216	
   217	#[public]
   218	impl IAccessControl for Example {
   219	    type Error = Error;
   220	
   221	    fn has_role(&self, role: B256, account: Address) -> bool {
   222	        self.access.has_role(role, account)
   223	    }
   224	
   225	    fn only_role(&self, role: B256) -> Result<(), Self::Error> {
   226	        Ok(self.access.only_role(role)?)
   227	    }
   228	
   229	    fn get_role_admin(&self, role: B256) -> B256 {
   230	        self.access.get_role_admin(role)
   231	    }
   232	
   233	    fn grant_role(
   234	        &mut self,
   235	        role: B256,
   236	        account: Address,
   237	    ) -> Result<(), Self::Error> {
   238	        Ok(self.access.grant_role(role, account)?)
   239	    }
   240	
   241	    fn revoke_role(
   242	        &mut self,
   243	        role: B256,
   244	        account: Address,
   245	    ) -> Result<(), Self::Error> {
   246	        Ok(self.access.revoke_role(role, account)?)
   247	    }
   248	
   249	    fn renounce_role(
   250	        &mut self,
   251	        role: B256,
   252	        confirmation: Address,
   253	    ) -> Result<(), Self::Error> {
   254	        Ok(self.access.renounce_role(role, confirmation)?)
   255	    }
   256	}
   257	----
   258	
   259	NOTE: Make sure you fully understand how https://docs.rs/openzeppelin-stylus/0.3.0/openzeppelin_stylus/access/control/struct.AccessControl.html[`AccessControl`] works before using it on your system, or copy-pasting the examples from this guide.
   260	
   261	While clear and explicit, this isn't anything we wouldn't have been able to achieve with `Ownable`. Indeed, where `AccessControl` shines is in scenarios where granular permissions are required, which can be implemented by defining _multiple_ roles.
   262	
   263	Let's augment our ERC-20 token example by also defining a 'burner' role, which lets accounts destroy tokens, and by using the `only_role` modifier:
   264	
   265	[source,rust]
   266	----
   267	use openzeppelin_stylus::{
   268	    access::control::{self, AccessControl, IAccessControl},
   269	    token::erc20::{self, Erc20, IErc20},
   270	};
   271	
   272	#[derive(SolidityError, Debug)]
   273	enum Error {
   274	    AccessControl(control::Error),
   275	    Erc20(erc20::Error),
   276	}
   277	
   278	#[entrypoint]
   279	#[storage]
   280	struct Example {
   281	    erc20: Erc20,
   282	    access: AccessControl,
   283	}
   284	
   285	const MINTER_ROLE: [u8; 32] =
   286	    keccak_const::Keccak256::new().update(b"MINTER_ROLE").finalize();
   287	
   288	const BURNER_ROLE: [u8; 32] =
   289	    keccak_const::Keccak256::new().update(b"BURNER_ROLE").finalize();
   290	
   291	#[public]
   292	#[implements(IErc20<Error = Error>, IAccessControl<Error = Error>)]
   293	impl Example {
   294	    fn mint(&mut self, to: Address, amount: U256) -> Result<(), Error> {
   295	        self.access.only_role(MINTER_ROLE.into())?;
   296	        self.erc20._mint(to, amount)?;
   297	        Ok(())
   298	    }
   299	
   300	    fn burn(&mut self, from: Address, amount: U256) -> Result<(), Error> {
   301	        self.access.only_role(BURNER_ROLE.into())?;
   302	        self.erc20._burn(from, amount)?;
   303	        Ok(())
   304	    }
   305	}
   306	
   307	#[public]
   308	impl IErc20 for Example {
   309	    // ...
   310	}
   311	
   312	#[public]
   313	impl IAccessControl for Example {
   314	    // ...
   315	}
   316	----
   317	
   318	So clean! By splitting concerns this way, more granular levels of permission may be implemented than were possible with the simpler _ownership_ approach to access control. Limiting what each component of a system is able to do is known as the https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Principle_of_least_privilege[principle of least privilege], and is a good security practice. Note that each account may still have more than one role, if so desired.
   319	
   320	[[granting-and-revoking]]
   321	=== Granting and Revoking Roles
   322	
   323	The ERC-20 token example above uses `_grant_role`, an `internal` function that is useful when programmatically assigning roles (such as during construction). But what if we later want to grant the 'minter' role to additional accounts?
   324	
   325	By default, **accounts with a role cannot grant it or revoke it from other accounts**: all having a role does is making the `has_role` check pass. To grant and revoke roles dynamically, you will need help from the _role's admin_.
   326	
   327	Every role has an associated admin role, which grants permission to call the `grant_role` and `revoke_role` functions. A role can be granted or revoked by using these if the calling account has the corresponding admin role. Multiple roles may have the same admin role to make management easier. A role's admin can even be the same role itself, which would cause accounts with that role to be able to also grant and revoke it.
   328	
   329	This mechanism can be used to create complex permissioning structures resembling organizational charts, but it also provides an easy way to manage simpler applications. `AccessControl` includes a special role, called `DEFAULT_ADMIN_ROLE`, which acts as the **default admin role for all roles**. An account with this role will be able to manage any other role, unless `_set_role_admin` is used to select a new admin role.
   330	
   331	Note that, by default, no accounts are granted the 'minter' or 'burner' roles. We assume you use a constructor to set the default admin role as the role of the deployer, or have a different mechanism where you make sure that you are able to grant roles. However, because those roles' admin role is the default admin role, and _that_ role was granted to `msg::sender()`, that same account can call `grant_role` to give minting or burning permission, and `revoke_role` to remove it.
   332	
   333	Dynamic role allocation is often a desirable property, for example in systems where trust in a participant may vary over time. It can also be used to support use cases such as https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Know_your_customer[KYC], where the list of role-bearers may not be known up-front, or may be prohibitively expensive to include in a single transaction.
=================== vesting-wallet.adoc
     1	= VestingWallet
     2	
     3	A vesting wallet is an ownable contract that can receive native currency and
     4	ERC-20 tokens, and release these assets to the wallet owner, also referred to as
     5	"beneficiary", according to a vesting schedule.
     6	
     7	Any assets transferred to this contract will follow the vesting schedule as if
     8	they were locked from the beginning. Consequently, if the vesting has already
     9	started, any amount of tokens sent to this contract will (at least partly) be
    10	immediately releasable.
    11	
    12	By setting the duration to 0, one can configure this contract to behave like
    13	an asset timelock that hold tokens for a beneficiary until a specified time.
    14	
    15	[NOTE]
    16	====
    17	Since the wallet is xref:access-control.adoc#ownership-and-ownable[Ownable],
    18	and ownership can be transferred, it is possible to sell unvested tokens.
    19	Preventing this in a smart contract is difficult, considering that: 1) a
    20	beneficiary address could be a counterfactually deployed contract, 2)
    21	there is likely to be a migration path for EOAs to become contracts in the near
    22	future.
    23	====
    24	
    25	[NOTE]
    26	====
    27	When using this contract with any token whose balance is adjusted automatically
    28	(i.e. a rebase token), make sure to account the supply/balance adjustment in the
    29	vesting schedule to ensure the vested amount is as intended.
    30	====
    31	
    32	[NOTE]
    33	====
    34	Chains with support for native ERC20s may allow the vesting wallet to withdraw
    35	the underlying asset as both an ERC20 and as native currency. For example, if
    36	chain C supports token A and the wallet gets deposited 100 A, then at 50% of
    37	the vesting period, the beneficiary can withdraw 50 A as ERC20 and 25 A as
    38	native currency (totaling 75 A). Consider disabling one of the withdrawal methods.
    39	====
    40	
    41	
    42	
    43	[[usage]]
    44	== Usage
    45	
    46	In order to make https://docs.rs/openzeppelin-stylus/0.3.0/openzeppelin_stylus/finance/vesting_wallet/index.html[`VestingWallet`] methods “external” so that other contracts can call them, you need to implement them by yourself for your final contract as follows:
    47	
    48	[source,rust]
    49	----
    50	use openzeppelin_stylus::finance::vesting_wallet::{
    51	    self, IVestingWallet, VestingWallet,
    52	};
    53	
    54	#[entrypoint]
    55	#[storage]
    56	struct VestingWalletExample {
    57	    vesting_wallet: VestingWallet,
    58	}
    59	
    60	#[public]
    61	#[implements(IVestingWallet<Error = vesting_wallet::Error>)]
    62	impl VestingWalletExample {
    63	    #[constructor]
    64	    fn constructor(
    65	        &mut self,
    66	        beneficiary: Address,
    67	        start_timestamp: U64,
    68	        duration_seconds: U64,
    69	    ) -> Result<(), vesting_wallet::Error> {
    70	        self.vesting_wallet.constructor(
    71	            beneficiary,
    72	            start_timestamp,
    73	            duration_seconds,
    74	        )
    75	    }
    76	
    77	    #[receive]
    78	    fn receive(&mut self) -> Result<(), Vec<u8>> {
    79	        self.vesting_wallet.receive()
    80	    }
    81	}
    82	
    83	#[public]
    84	impl IVestingWallet for VestingWalletExample {
    85	    type Error = vesting_wallet::Error;
    86	
    87	    fn owner(&self) -> Address {
    88	        self.vesting_wallet.owner()
    89	    }
    90	
    91	    fn transfer_ownership(
    92	        &mut self,
    93	        new_owner: Address,
    94	    ) -> Result<(), Self::Error> {
    95	        self.vesting_wallet.transfer_ownership(new_owner)
    96	    }
    97	
    98	    fn renounce_ownership(
    99	        &mut self,
   100	    ) -> Result<(), Self::Error> {
   101	        self.vesting_wallet.renounce_ownership()
   102	    }
   103	
   104	    fn start(&self) -> U256 {
   105	        self.vesting_wallet.start()
   106	    }
   107	
   108	    fn duration(&self) -> U256 {
   109	        self.vesting_wallet.duration()
   110	    }
   111	
   112	    fn end(&self) -> U256 {
   113	        self.vesting_wallet.end()
   114	    }
   115	
   116	    #[selector(name = "released")]
   117	    fn released_eth(&self) -> U256 {
   118	        self.vesting_wallet.released_eth()
   119	    }
   120	
   121	    #[selector(name = "released")]
   122	    fn released_erc20(&self, token: Address) -> U256 {
   123	        self.vesting_wallet.released_erc20(token)
   124	    }
   125	
   126	    #[selector(name = "releasable")]
   127	    fn releasable_eth(&self) -> U256 {
   128	        self.vesting_wallet.releasable_eth()
   129	    }
   130	
   131	    #[selector(name = "releasable")]
   132	    fn releasable_erc20(
   133	        &mut self,
   134	        token: Address,
   135	    ) -> Result<U256, Self::Error> {
   136	        self.vesting_wallet.releasable_erc20(token)
   137	    }
   138	
   139	    #[selector(name = "release")]
   140	    fn release_eth(&mut self) -> Result<(), Self::Error> {
   141	        self.vesting_wallet.release_eth()
   142	    }
   143	
   144	    #[selector(name = "release")]
   145	    fn release_erc20(
   146	        &mut self,
   147	        token: Address,
   148	    ) -> Result<(), Self::Error> {
   149	        self.vesting_wallet.release_erc20(token)
   150	    }
   151	
   152	    #[selector(name = "vestedAmount")]
   153	    fn vested_amount_eth(&self, timestamp: u64) -> U256 {
   154	        self.vesting_wallet.vested_amount_eth(timestamp)
   155	    }
   156	
   157	    #[selector(name = "vestedAmount")]
   158	    fn vested_amount_erc20(
   159	        &mut self,
   160	        token: Address,
   161	        timestamp: u64,
   162	    ) -> Result<U256, Self::Error> {
   163	        self.vesting_wallet.vested_amount_erc20(token, timestamp)
   164	    }
   165	}
   166	----
